lessons.title: Route Planning and Optimization
lessons.body: Route planning is about finding the best path for your vehicle from point A to B, considering distance, time, cost, and safety. In Africa, road conditions vary wildly: a paved highway may be faster but has tolls, while a dirt road is free but slow and risky in the rainy season. Start by mapping all your stops on a paper map or using free tools like Google Maps. Then, group stops by area. For example, if you deliver to 10 shops in Nairobi, plan a loop that covers Westlands, then Parklands, then CBD, avoiding backtracking. A simple rule: never cross your own path. For more complex routes, use route optimization software like Routific (free trial) or Circuit for Teams. These tools consider traffic, vehicle size, and delivery windows. In Lagos, traffic can double travel time during rush hour (7-10am and 4-8pm), so schedule deliveries outside those times. Also, consider security: avoid known hijacking hotspots like certain stretches of the N3 in South Africa. Always have a backup route in case of accidents or protests. For small businesses, a daily route plan saved on a phone can save 20-30% on fuel. Train your drivers to use GPS apps like Google Maps or Waze, but also teach them to read road signs and ask locals. Remember, the shortest route is not always the fastest or safest. Test different routes for a week, record time and fuel, then choose the best. Finally, update your routes weekly as new customers or road closures appear.

lessons.title: Load Planning and Consolidation
lessons.body: Load planning is deciding what goes on a truck, in what order, and how to arrange it. Consolidation means combining multiple small shipments into one full truckload to save money. For example, if you have 5 customers each needing 2 tonnes of goods from Mombasa to Nairobi, instead of sending 5 small trucks, you send one 10-tonne truck and split the cost. This cuts fuel, driver wages, and tolls by up to 60%. Start by knowing your vehicle's capacity: a typical 10-tonne truck has about 30 cubic meters of space. Weigh and measure every item. Heavy items go at the bottom, near the axles; light items on top. Fragile goods like electronics go in the middle, away from doors. Use pallets and straps to prevent shifting. In Africa, many roads are bumpy, so secure loads tightly. For load planning, use a simple spreadsheet: list each item, weight, dimensions, and destination. Then, use free software like EasyCargo or Excel Solver to optimize. If you don't have software, use the 'first-fit' method: start with the biggest items, then fill gaps with smaller ones. For consolidation, set a cut-off time each day (e.g., 2pm) for customers to book space on tomorrow's truck. Offer a discount for flexible delivery windows. Also, consider backhauling: instead of returning empty, find goods to bring back. For instance, a truck delivering maize to Nairobi can return with manufactured goods from Nairobi to Mombasa. This doubles revenue per trip. Always check axle weight limits to avoid fines. In Kenya, the maximum legal load per axle is 8 tonnes. Overloading damages roads and risks accidents. Train your loaders to follow a loading plan diagram. A well-loaded truck saves fuel, time, and prevents damage.

lessons.title: Scheduling and Dispatch Operations
lessons.body: Scheduling is assigning specific times for pickups and deliveries. Dispatch is sending drivers out with instructions. Together, they keep your fleet moving efficiently. Start with a daily schedule. For example, if you have 3 trucks and 15 deliveries, assign each truck 5 deliveries in a logical order. Use a whiteboard or free tools like Google Sheets or Trello. Set realistic time windows: a delivery in a busy market like Kariakoo in Dar es Salaam might take 30 minutes to navigate, while a warehouse on the outskirts takes 10 minutes. Add buffer time for traffic, breakdowns, and paperwork. A good rule: add 20% extra time to every trip. Dispatch involves giving drivers a trip sheet with customer names, addresses, contact numbers, delivery times, and special instructions. Also, give them a phone with airtime and a charger. In Africa, network coverage can be spotty, so download offline maps. Use WhatsApp groups for real-time updates: drivers send a message when they leave, arrive, and complete each stop. For larger fleets, use dispatch software like Track-POD or Onfleet. These let you assign jobs, track drivers, and send notifications to customers. Schedule drivers' shifts legally: in most African countries, drivers must rest after 8 hours of driving. Plan for two drivers on long hauls. Also, schedule vehicle maintenance: every 5,000 km for oil changes, and daily checks for tires, brakes, and lights. A breakdown costs more than preventive maintenance. For dispatch, prioritize urgent deliveries but don't overload one driver. Rotate routes so drivers don't get bored or complacent. Finally, review your schedule at the end of each day: what went wrong? Adjust for tomorrow. Consistency builds customer trust.

lessons.title: Intermodal and Multimodal Transport
lessons.body: Intermodal transport means using two or more modes of transport (e.g., truck, train, ship) without handling the goods themselves when changing modes. Multimodal is similar but the same company handles the entire journey under one contract. For example, you can move a container from Mombasa to Kampala by ship to Mombasa, then train to Nairobi, then truck to Kampala. This is often cheaper and greener than trucking all the way. In Africa, key corridors include the Northern Corridor (Mombasa-Kampala-Kigali) and the Central Corridor (Dar es Salaam-Kigali-Bujumbura). Using rail for long distances saves 30-50% on fuel and reduces road wear. But rail can be slow and unreliable. So, plan for delays: keep extra inventory. For intermodal, you need containers (20ft or 40ft) and a truck with a container chassis. At each transfer point, a crane lifts the container. You must pay terminal handling charges. For example, at the Port of Mombasa, handling a 20ft container costs about $200. Always get a through bill of lading from a freight forwarder. They handle customs, documentation, and coordination. For small businesses, you can consolidate your goods with others in a container to save costs. Use platforms like iContainers or Freightos to compare rates. When choosing intermodal, calculate total cost: trucking to port, ocean freight, rail, trucking to final destination, plus fees. Sometimes trucking directly is cheaper for short distances. But for over 1,000 km, intermodal usually wins. Also consider time: a truck from Mombasa to Kampala takes 5-7 days; intermodal takes 10-14 days. So match mode to urgency. Always insure your goods; intermodal has more handling points, increasing risk of damage. Train your staff on container packing and customs procedures.

lessons.title: Last-Mile Delivery Strategies
lessons.body: Last-mile delivery is the final step from a hub to the customer's door. It's the most expensive part of the supply chain, often 40-50% of total cost. In Africa, challenges include poor addresses, traffic, and cash-on-delivery. To succeed, use a hub-and-spoke model: a central warehouse in each city, with smaller satellites in neighborhoods. For example, in Accra, have a main hub in Tema and satellites in Osu, Madina, and Achimota. Use motorcycles for small packages: they're faster in traffic and cheaper to run. A motorcycle can do 30-40 deliveries per day, while a van does 15-20. For larger items, use vans or trucks. Optimize by clustering deliveries: group orders by area and time. Offer customers a 2-hour delivery window and send an SMS with a tracking link. Use free tools like Google My Maps to plot stops. For cash-on-delivery, equip riders with mobile money (M-Pesa, MTN MoMo) and a secure cash box. Reconcile cash daily. Address problems: many customers don't have street addresses. Use landmarks: 'near the blue church' or 'opposite the market'. Ask for a phone number and call when nearby. For failed deliveries, have a return policy and reschedule. Consider pickup points: partner with local shops or kiosks where customers can collect. This reduces cost and increases convenience. In Nairobi, Sendy and Lori use this model. For perishables, use insulated bags. Track rider performance: on-time rate, cost per delivery, customer rating. Pay incentives for high performance. Finally, communicate proactively: if a delivery is late, call the customer. A happy customer forgives delays; an angry one doesn't. Keep learning: test new routes, new vehicles, new technologies.

lessons.title: Real-Time Tracking and Exception Management
lessons.body: Real-time tracking means knowing where your vehicles and goods are at any moment. Exception management means handling problems like delays, breakdowns, or accidents. Start with GPS trackers. Basic trackers cost $20-50 and send location every 30 seconds. Install them in all vehicles. Use free apps like Google Maps Location Sharing for a cheap start, but for business, use platforms like Traccar (open-source) or Wialon. These show speed, fuel level, and history. Set up geofences: virtual boundaries around key locations (warehouse, customer sites). When a vehicle enters or leaves, you get an alert. This helps prevent theft and unauthorized stops. For cargo, use Bluetooth temperature sensors for perishables. If temperature goes above 8Â°C, you get an alert. For exception management, create a protocol. For example: if a truck breaks down, driver calls dispatch. Dispatch sends nearest mechanic and a backup vehicle if needed. Inform the customer of the delay and new ETA. Record the incident. For accidents, ensure driver safety first, then police report, then insurance. For lost packages, use tracking to locate last known position. In Africa, network gaps are common, so trackers should store data offline and upload when back online. Train drivers to use the system and not tamper with it. Use data to improve: analyze frequent breakdown spots, traffic jams, and theft areas. Share insights with drivers. Offer bonuses for zero exceptions. For customers, provide a tracking link via SMS or WhatsApp. This reduces calls to your office. Tools like Samsara and Verizon Connect are expensive; local options like iTrack Africa or Cartrack are more affordable. Start small: track one vehicle, learn, then expand. Real-time tracking pays for itself by reducing fuel theft, improving customer service, and optimizing routes.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Transportation Planning and Execution in African Agribusiness

Transportation planning and execution is where agribusiness margins are won or lost across Africa. Whether you are moving maize from a warehouse in Nakuru to a mill in Nairobi, cocoa from a cooperative in Kumasi to Tema Port, or fresh produce from a farm in Limpopo to a cold store in Johannesburg, the way you plan routes, load vehicles, schedule dispatches, and manage exceptions determines your cost per tonne-kilometre, your product quality on arrival, and your reputation with buyers.

This practical reference consolidates the six core lessons of this module into an operational tool you can use daily. It focuses on decisions that reduce cost, protect cargo, and keep customers informed. Every table, diagram, and checklist below is designed for the realities of African road, rail, and intermodal corridors: long distances, variable road quality, border delays, informal last-mile networks, and limited cold-chain infrastructure.

1. Route Planning and Optimization

Route planning is not just about finding the shortest path. For agribusiness, it is about finding the lowest total cost path that preserves product quality and meets delivery windows. Key variables include road condition, axle load limits, toll costs, fuel availability, security risk, and seasonal factors such as rain and harvest traffic.

Use a structured approach: map all feasible routes, estimate time and cost per route, score each route on reliability and risk, then select the best option for each load type. For high-value or perishable cargo, reliability usually outweighs a shorter but unpredictable route.

2. Load Planning and Consolidation

Load planning determines how much cargo you move per trip and how safely it travels. In African agribusiness, poor load planning leads to damaged produce, overweight fines, and wasted capacity. Consolidationâcombining smaller loads from multiple shippers or farmsâis one of the fastest ways to reduce cost per tonne, especially on backhaul routes.

Key principles: maximise payload within legal axle limits, stack according to product weight and fragility, separate incompatible goods (e.g., fresh produce and chemicals), and use load bars, straps, and pallets to prevent movement. For cold chain, ensure airflow around pallets and pre-cool the vehicle before loading.

Table 1: Typical Load Capacity and Cost Indicators for Common African Agribusiness Vehicles
Vehicle Type Typical Payload Best Use Indicative Cost per km (USD) Key Risk
7-tonne rigid truck 6â7 tonnes Farm-to-warehouse, short regional 0.45â0.70 Overloading, poor road access
28-tonne semi-trailer 25â28 tonnes Long-haul dry bulk, corridor transport 0.90â1.40 Border delays, axle load fines
Refrigerated 10-tonne truck 8â10 tonnes Perishables, dairy, meat, flowers 1.10â1.70 Cold chain breaks, fuel cost
40-ft container on rail 25â28 tonnes Port-to-inland corridor, bulk export 0.35â0.60 Schedule reliability, terminal delays
Pick-up / 1-tonne van 0.8â1.2 tonnes Last-mile urban delivery 0.25â0.45 Traffic, theft, multiple drops

Source: Compiled from the World Bank Logistics Performance Index (2023), the African Development Bank Transport Sector Reports (2022), and industry operator data from East and West African corridors.

3. Scheduling and Dispatch Operations

Scheduling is the bridge between plan and execution. It assigns vehicles, drivers, and loads to specific times and routes. Dispatch is the control point that releases vehicles and tracks them until delivery. In agribusiness, scheduling must account for harvest windows, market days, port cut-off times, and driver rest regulations.

Use a dispatch board or transport management system (TMS) to record: vehicle ID, driver, load details, departure time, expected arrival, route, and contact numbers. Confirm loading completion before dispatch. Brief drivers on route, delivery point, and exception contacts. Never dispatch a vehicle without a signed waybill, load inspection, and fuel/tyre check.

4. Intermodal and Multimodal Transport

Intermodal transport uses more than one modeâtypically road plus rail or road plus inland waterwayâunder a single contract. Multimodal adds a single operator responsible for the entire journey. In Africa, intermodal is most developed on corridors such as MombasaâNairobiâKampala, DurbanâJohannesburg, and AbidjanâOuagadougou.

Benefits include lower long-haul cost, reduced road wear, and larger payloads. Challenges include terminal handling delays, documentation, and coordination between rail and road operators. For agribusiness, intermodal works best for non-perishable bulk commodities such as maize, fertiliser, and cement, where schedule flexibility exists.

5. Last-Mile Delivery Strategies

Last-mile delivery is the most expensive and most visible part of the chain. In African cities, it involves traffic congestion, informal addresses, security concerns, and small drop sizes. Strategies that work include: route densification (grouping nearby deliveries), time-window delivery, use of motorcycles or three-wheelers for narrow roads, and local micro-hubs to shorten final legs.

For fresh produce, last-mile must protect cold chain and product integrity. Use insulated boxes, avoid open pick-up beds in hot weather, and train drivers on handling. For urban food distribution, consider night delivery to avoid traffic and reduce spoilage.

6. Real-Time Tracking and Exception Management

Real-time tracking uses GPS, telematics, and mobile apps to monitor vehicle location, speed, temperature, and door status. Exception management is the process of detecting and responding to deviations: breakdowns, delays, temperature breaches, accidents, theft, or border hold-ups.

Set clear exception thresholds: e.g., delay over 2 hours, temperature above 8Â°C for chilled goods, route deviation over 5 km, or unscheduled stop over 30 minutes. Define escalation contacts and response actions. Record every exception and review weekly to improve planning.

Table 2: Common Transport Exceptions in African Agribusiness and Recommended Responses
Exception Typical Cause Immediate Response Preventive Action
Border delay > 6 hours Documentation, inspection, congestion Notify customer, arrange overnight security, update ETA Pre-clear documents, use authorised customs agents, avoid peak days
Temperature breach Reefer failure, door left open, fuel shortage Divert to nearest cold store, isolate affected cargo, inform buyer Pre-trip reefer check, fuel monitoring, driver training
Vehicle breakdown Poor maintenance, bad roads, overload Dispatch rescue vehicle, transload cargo, secure site Preventive maintenance schedule, roadside assistance contract
Route deviation Driver choice, road closure, theft risk Contact driver, verify reason, reroute if needed Geofencing alerts, driver briefings, route risk maps
Delivery rejection Quality failure, wrong quantity, late arrival Document reason, arrange return or disposal, notify operations Pre-dispatch quality check, customer confirmation, accurate scheduling

Source: Adapted from the Global Alliance for Trade Facilitation, Border Delay Case Studies (2022), and the Cool Chain Association, Cold Chain Exception Management Guidelines (2021).

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Overloading and Load Security

Overloading is a leading cause of road accidents, axle failure, and cargo damage in African agribusiness transport. Never exceed the vehicle's gross vehicle mass (GVM) or axle load limits. Ensure all loads are secured with straps, load bars, or tarpaulins before departure. Unsecured produce can shift on corners, injure the driver, and spill onto roads. For perishables, never block airflow vents in refrigerated vehicles. Conduct a pre-departure load inspection and record it. If in doubt, reduce the loadâno delivery is worth a life.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Route confirmed: Best route selected based on cost, reliability, cargo type, and current road/border conditions.
  2. Load plan verified: Payload within legal limits, cargo secured, incompatible goods separated, cold chain airflow clear.
  3. Vehicle and driver ready: Pre-trip inspection done, fuel and tyres checked, driver briefed on route and delivery point.
  4. Documents complete: Waybill, delivery note, permits, customs papers, and contact numbers on board.
  5. Dispatch recorded: Departure time, expected arrival, and tracking details logged in dispatch board or TMS.
  6. Tracking active: GPS or telematics on, exception thresholds set, escalation contacts known.
  7. Customer informed: Buyer or receiver notified of dispatch, ETA, and any expected delays.
  8. Exception log updated: Any deviation recorded with cause, response, and preventive action for review.

Further Reading

  • World Bank â Connecting to Compete: Trade Logistics in the Global Economy (Logistics Performance Index 2023)
  • African Development Bank â Study on Road Transport Connectivity in Africa
  • FAO â Food Loss Reduction and Cold Chain Development in Africa
  • Global Alliance for Trade Facilitation â Border and Corridor Case Studies
  • International Road Transport Union (IRU) â Road Transport and Logistics Resources

This practical reference is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills course: Transport and Logistics Business â Module: Transportation Planning and Execution. Use it alongside your operational data and local regulations. Always verify current border, customs, and road conditions before dispatch.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of route planning?
options: A) To use the shortest distance always
B) To find the best path considering time, cost, and safety
C) To avoid all toll roads
D) To drive as fast as possible
quiz.explanation: Route planning balances multiple factors, not just distance.

quiz.q: In Africa, why might a longer route be better than a shorter one?
options: A) Longer routes have better scenery
B) Shorter routes may have poor road conditions or security risks
C) Longer routes always have less traffic
D) Shorter routes are more expensive
quiz.explanation: Road quality and safety can make a longer route faster and cheaper.

quiz.q: What is a simple rule to avoid backtracking in route planning?
options: B) Never cross your own path
quiz.explanation: Crossing your own path means you are retracing steps, wasting time and fuel.

quiz.q: Which tool can help optimize complex routes?
quiz.explanation: Routific is a route optimization software.

quiz.q: What is load consolidation?
options: A) Combining multiple small shipments into one full truckload
quiz.explanation: Consolidation means grouping shipments to maximize vehicle capacity and reduce costs.

quiz.q: Where should heavy items be placed in a truck?
options: A) On top of light items
B) At the bottom, near the axles
quiz.explanation: Heavy items at the bottom improve stability and safety.

quiz.q: What is backhauling?
options: B) Finding goods to transport on the return trip
quiz.explanation: Backhauling uses the return trip to carry goods, increasing revenue.

quiz.q: What is the maximum legal load per axle in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: Kenya's legal axle load limit is 8 tonnes to protect roads.

quiz.q: What is the difference between scheduling and dispatch?
options: A) Scheduling assigns times; dispatch sends drivers out
B) Scheduling is for trucks; dispatch is for trains
D) Scheduling is done by drivers; dispatch by customers
quiz.explanation: Scheduling sets the plan; dispatch executes it.

quiz.q: How much buffer time should you add to each trip?
quiz.explanation: Adding 20% buffer accounts for traffic and unexpected delays.

quiz.q: What is a key legal requirement for drivers in most African countries?
options: B) Rest after 8 hours of driving
quiz.explanation: Drivers must rest to prevent fatigue and accidents.

quiz.q: How often should you check vehicle tires and brakes?
quiz.explanation: Daily checks catch problems early and prevent breakdowns.

quiz.q: What is intermodal transport?
options: A) Using one mode of transport
B) Using two or more modes without handling goods
quiz.explanation: Intermodal uses multiple modes, with containers transferred between them.

quiz.q: Which corridor connects Mombasa to Kampala?
quiz.explanation: The Northern Corridor runs from Mombasa through Kenya to Uganda and beyond.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of intermodal transport?
quiz.explanation: Rail and sea are cheaper per tonne-km than road for long hauls.

quiz.q: What document covers the entire intermodal journey?
quiz.explanation: A through bill of lading covers all modes under one contract.

quiz.q: What is last-mile delivery?
options: A) The first step from factory
B) The final step to the customer
quiz.explanation: Last-mile is the final leg from hub to customer.

quiz.q: Why are motorcycles often used for last-mile delivery in Africa?
options: A) They can carry more than trucks
B) They are faster in traffic and cheaper to run
quiz.explanation: Motorcycles navigate congested streets efficiently.

quiz.q: What is a common challenge in last-mile delivery in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Many areas lack formal street addresses, requiring landmarks.

quiz.q: What is a pickup point?
options: A) A place where customers collect their orders
quiz.explanation: Pickup points are local shops where customers can collect packages.

quiz.q: What is real-time tracking?
options: A) Knowing where vehicles and goods are at any moment
B) Tracking only at the end of the day
quiz.explanation: Real-time tracking provides live location updates.

quiz.q: What is a geofence?
options: B) A virtual boundary that triggers alerts
quiz.explanation: Geofences alert you when a vehicle enters or leaves an area.

quiz.q: What should a driver do first in case of an accident?
quiz.explanation: Safety of people comes first, then report and document.

quiz.q: Why are offline capabilities important for GPS trackers in Africa?
options: B) Because network coverage can be spotty
quiz.explanation: Trackers store data when offline and upload when back in coverage.

quiz.q: What is an exception in logistics?
options: B) A problem like delay or breakdown
quiz.explanation: Exceptions are deviations from the plan that require action.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of real-time tracking?
quiz.explanation: Tracking deters fuel theft and unauthorized stops.

quiz.q: Which of these is a local African tracking provider?
quiz.explanation: Cartrack operates in Africa and is more affordable.

quiz.q: What should you do if a delivery is going to be late?
quiz.explanation: Proactive communication maintains trust.

quiz.q: What is a key metric for last-mile delivery performance?
quiz.explanation: On-time rate measures reliability.

quiz.q: What is the first step in load planning?
quiz.explanation: Knowing capacity prevents overloading and ensures efficient use of space.
